title: Polymorphism
content: Polymorphism in C# allows objects to be treated as instances of their base type while invoking derived implementations at runtime. Achieved with virtual/override and interfaces.
example: class Animal { public virtual void Speak() {} } class Dog : Animal { public override void Speak() => Console.WriteLine("Woof"); } Animal a = new Dog(); a.Speak();

title: Inheritance
content: Inheritance lets a class (derived) reuse members of another class (base), enabling code reuse and an is-a relationship.
example: class Base { public void M() {} } class Derived : Base { } var d = new Derived(); d.M();

title: Encapsulation
content: Encapsulation hides internal state and exposes behavior via public members; access modifiers (private/protected/public) enforce it.
example: class Person { private int age; public int Age { get => age; set => age = value; } }

title: Abstraction
content: Abstraction exposes only necessary details and hides implementation. Use abstract classes or interfaces to define contracts.
example: abstract class Shape { public abstract double Area(); } class Circle : Shape { public double R; public override double Area() => Math.PI*R*R; }

title: Interface
content: An interface defines a contract of members (methods/properties/events) without implementation. Types implement interfaces to provide behavior.
example: interface ILogger { void Log(string msg); } class ConsoleLogger : ILogger { public void Log(string msg) => Console.WriteLine(msg); }

title: Delegate
content: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer. Delegates are used for callbacks and form the basis of events.
example: delegate void Notify(string message); Notify n = msg => Console.WriteLine(msg); n("hello");

title: Event
content: Events provide a publish-subscribe mechanism built on delegates, allowing a class to notify subscribers when something happens.
example: public class Button { public event EventHandler Clicked; void OnClick() => Clicked?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty); }

title: LINQ
content: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) provides query capabilities over collections and data sources using IEnumerable/IQueryable with fluent or query syntax.
example: var evens = numbers.Where(n => n % 2 == 0).ToList();

title: Generics
content: Generics enable type-safe data structures and methods without committing to a concrete type at compile time, reducing casts and runtime errors.
example: List<int> list = new List<int>(); list.Add(42);

title: Async/Await
content: Async/await simplifies asynchronous programming by allowing asynchronous code to be written in a sequential style. Methods typically return Task or Task<T>.
example: async Task Load() { var res = await httpClient.GetStringAsync(url); Console.WriteLine(res); }

title: Value vs Reference Types
content: Value types (structs, primitives) are copied on assignment and stored on the stack; reference types (classes) are references to heap objects. Mutating a copy of a value type does not affect the original.
example: int a = 1; int b = a; b = 2; // a == 1; class C { public int X; } C c1 = new C{X=1}; C c2 = c1; c2.X = 2; // c1.X == 2

title: Boxing and Unboxing
content: Boxing converts a value type to object/reference type; unboxing extracts the value type from the object. Boxing/unboxing has performance costs.
example: object o = 123; int i = (int)o; // boxing when assigning, unboxing when casting

title: Nullable Types
content: Nullable value types (T?) allow value types to represent null. Use HasValue/Value or the null-coalescing/conditional operators.
example: int? n = null; if (n.HasValue) Console.WriteLine(n.Value); int m = n ?? 0;

title: Extension Methods
content: Extension methods add methods to existing types without modifying them, by defining a static method in a static class with the 'this' modifier on the first parameter.
example: public static class StrExt { public static bool IsNullOrEmpty(this string s) => string.IsNullOrEmpty(s); } string s = null; bool ok = s.IsNullOrEmpty();

title: Partial Classes
content: Partial classes allow splitting a class definition across multiple files — useful for code generation and separation of concerns.
example: // File1.cs: public partial class MyClass { void A() {} } // File2.cs: public partial class MyClass { void B() {} }

title: Struct vs Class
content: Structs are value types (no inheritance, lightweight) and good for small immutable data; classes are reference types with full OO features.
example: struct Point { public int X, Y; } Point p1 = new Point{X=1}; Point p2 = p1; p2.X=2; // p1.X == 1

title: IDisposable and using
content: IDisposable defines Dispose() for releasing unmanaged resources. The 'using' statement ensures Dispose is called even on exceptions.
example: using(var s = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open)) { /* use stream */ } // Dispose called automatically

title: Records (C# 9+)
content: Records provide immutable reference types with built-in value equality, concise syntax for DTOs and pattern matching support.
example: public record Person(string Name, int Age); var p = new Person("Alice",30); var p2 = p with { Age = 31 };

title: Pattern Matching
content: Pattern matching enables concise type checks and deconstruction in switch/if expressions (is, switch, relational and positional patterns).
example: if (obj is Person p) Console.WriteLine(p.Name); switch(x) { case int n when n>0: break; }

title: Covariance and Contravariance
content: Covariance allows implicit conversion of generic types for output positions (e.g., IEnumerable<Derived> to IEnumerable<Base>), contravariance for input positions (e.g., Action<Base> to Action<Derived>).
example: IEnumerable<string> s = new List<string>(); IEnumerable<object> o = s; // covariance

title: Garbage Collection
content: C# uses a generational garbage collector to manage memory. Developers should release unmanaged resources via IDisposable; forcing GC.Collect() is rarely needed.
example: class C { ~C() { /* finalizer */ } } // prefer implementing IDisposable for deterministic cleanup

title: Threading and TPL
content: The Task Parallel Library (TPL) and async/await simplify concurrent and parallel programming. Use Task, Task.Run, and synchronization primitives when needed.
example: var tasks = Enumerable.Range(1,5).Select(i => Task.Run(() => DoWork(i))); await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

title: Middleware (ASP.NET Core)
content: Middleware are components in the HTTP request pipeline that can handle requests and responses. You register middleware in Program.cs/Startup using app.UseXyz().
example: app.Use(async (context, next) => { Console.WriteLine("Before"); await next(); Console.WriteLine("After"); });

title: Kestrel vs IIS
content: Kestrel is the cross-platform web server for ASP.NET Core. In production it is often run behind a reverse proxy (IIS, Nginx) for additional features like process management or TLS termination.
example: In Docker: dotnet MyApp.dll (Kestrel serves requests directly).

title: Dependency Injection (DI)
content: ASP.NET Core has built-in dependency injection. Services are registered with lifetimes (Singleton, Scoped, Transient) and injected into constructors.
example: services.AddScoped<IRepo, Repo>(); public class C { public C(IRepo repo) { _repo=repo; } }

title: Configuration (appsettings.json)
content: Configuration in .NET Core is hierarchical and provider-based (JSON, environment, secrets, etc.). Bind strongly-typed objects using IConfiguration or options pattern.
example: builder.Configuration.GetSection("MySettings").Bind(mySettings); or services.Configure<MySettings>(Configuration.GetSection("MySettings"));

title: Logging (Microsoft.Extensions.Logging)
content: ASP.NET Core uses a logging abstraction with providers (Console, Debug, Seq, etc.). Inject ILogger<T> and log with structured messages.
example: public HomeController(ILogger<HomeController> log) { _log = log; } _log.LogInformation("User {UserId} logged in", userId);

title: Entity Framework Core (DbContext)
content: EF Core is the ORM for .NET Core. Define DbContext and DbSet<T>, configure via OnModelCreating or fluent API, and use LINQ to query.
example: public class AppDb : DbContext { public DbSet<User> Users { get; set; } } var users = await db.Users.Where(u=>u.Active).ToListAsync();

title: Migrations (EF Core)
content: Migrations manage schema changes. Use CLI commands to add and apply migrations which generate migration classes for schema evolution.
example: dotnet ef migrations add InitialCreate; dotnet ef database update

title: Minimal Hosting / Program.cs vs Startup.cs
content: ASP.NET Core supports minimal hosting model (single Program.cs) and the older Startup.cs pattern. Both configure services and the request pipeline.
example: var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); var app = builder.Build(); app.MapGet("/", ()=>"Hello"); app.Run();

title: Health Checks
content: Health checks provide endpoints to report app health. Register health checks and map endpoints for orchestration platforms to probe.
example: services.AddHealthChecks(); app.MapHealthChecks("/health");

title: Configuration for Production (Secrets & Env)
content: Use environment variables, Azure Key Vault or user-secrets for sensitive settings. Do not hard-code secrets in appsettings.json for production.
example: builder.Configuration.AddEnvironmentVariables(); var conn = builder.Configuration["ConnectionStrings:Default"];

title: Dockerizing ASP.NET Core
content: Package ASP.NET Core apps into containers using a Dockerfile that builds and publishes the app, then runs dotnet APP.dll in a runtime image.
example: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:7.0 WORKDIR /app COPY ./publish . ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet","MyApp.dll"]

title: IHostedService / BackgroundService
content: IHostedService is the interface for background tasks in Generic Host. BackgroundService is a base class that provides an ExecuteAsync loop with cancellation support. Use for long-running background work (workers, scheduled jobs).
example: public class Worker : BackgroundService { protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken) { while(!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested) { await DoWork(); await Task.Delay(1000, stoppingToken); } } }

title: Graceful shutdown and CancellationTokens
content: Host shutdown sends cancellation tokens to services and controllers. Respect CancellationToken in async work to allow graceful shutdown and resource cleanup (Dispose/IDisposable + IHostedService).
example: app.Lifetime.ApplicationStopping.Register(() => { /* cleanup */ }); // or accept CancellationToken in controllers/actions

title: Observability: OpenTelemetry and Distributed Tracing
content: Use OpenTelemetry for metrics, traces and logs. Instrument HTTP, EF Core, gRPC and custom spans to trace requests across services and visualize in systems like Jaeger/Zipkin/OTel Collector.
example: services.AddOpenTelemetryTracing(builder => builder.AddAspNetCore().AddHttpClient().AddJaegerExporter());

title: Structured logging and correlation IDs
content: Use ILogger with structured logs for rich, queryable events. Include correlation/request IDs to tie logs across services. Logging providers output JSON for central analysis (Seq/Elastic).
example: using (_logger.BeginScope(new { CorrelationId = traceId })) { _logger.LogInformation("Processing {OrderId}", orderId); }

title: Authentication & Authorization (JWT / OAuth2)
content: ASP.NET Core supports JWT bearer authentication and OAuth2 flows. Validate tokens, configure policies, and use scope/claims-based authorization for fine-grained access control.
example: services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme).AddJwtBearer(opts => { opts.Authority = "https://auth"; opts.Audience = "api"; }); [Authorize(Policy="AdminOnly")]

title: Data Protection and key management
content: DataProtection API handles encryption of cookies, tokens and keys. Configure key storage (file system, Azure blob, Redis) and automatic key rotation for multi-instance apps.
example: services.AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToFileSystem(new DirectoryInfo("/keys")).SetApplicationName("MyApp");

title: Performance tuning: GC, ThreadPool, and AOT
content: Tune .NET performance using Server GC, threadpool settings, ReadyToRun or Native AOT and publish trimming. Profile hot paths and avoid excessive allocations and blocking calls.
example: <RuntimeOptions> <GCServer enabled="true"/> </RuntimeOptions> // or dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishReadyToRun=true

title: gRPC in ASP.NET Core
content: gRPC uses HTTP/2 for high-performance RPC between services. ASP.NET Core supports gRPC services and clients; design proto contracts and leverage streaming for duplex scenarios.
example: endpoints.MapGrpcService<GreeterService>(); // proto: rpc SayHello (HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);

title: Distributed caching and Redis
content: Use a distributed cache (Redis) for shared state and session caching across instances. Cache with proper expiration and cache stampede mitigation strategies.
example: services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(opts => { opts.Configuration = "redis:6379"; opts.InstanceName = "MyApp"; }); await cache.SetStringAsync("key","val");

title: Message-driven architecture (RabbitMQ/Kafka) and idempotency
content: Use message brokers for async communication and resiliency. Ensure consumers are idempotent and handle duplicates. Use at-least-once delivery semantics with dead-lettering and retries.
example: bus.Publish(new OrderPlaced{Id=123}); // consumer checks if OrderProcessed(order.Id) before handling

title: Resilience patterns: Retry, Circuit Breaker (Polly)
content: Use Polly for transient-fault-handling (retry, circuit breaker, timeout, fallback). Combine with IHttpClientFactory to configure resiliency per external service.
example: services.AddHttpClient("api").AddTransientHttpErrorPolicy(p => p.WaitAndRetryAsync(3, i => TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)));

title: Health, readiness and liveness probes
content: Expose health endpoints for orchestration systems. Differentiate liveness (is process alive) from readiness (can serve traffic). Use health checks with tags and dependencies checks (DB, cache).
example: services.AddHealthChecks().AddSqlServer(conn).AddRedis(redis); app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready", new HealthCheckOptions{Predicate = rc => rc.Tags.Contains("ready")});

title: Observability: Metrics and Prometheus
content: Publish application metrics (response time, error rates) to Prometheus. Instrument middleware and libraries, expose /metrics endpoint, and use Grafana for dashboards.
example: services.AddPrometheusCounters(); app.UseMetricServer(); // exposes /metrics

title: Secrets management and secure deployments
content: Avoid storing secrets in source. Use environment variables, Azure Key Vault, or AWS Secrets Manager. Integrate CI/CD to inject secrets at deploy time and rotate regularly.
example: builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(new Uri(kvUrl), new DefaultAzureCredential()); var secret = config["MySecret"];

title: Deployment strategies: Blue/Green, Canary and zero-downtime
content: Use deployment strategies (blue/green, canary) and health checks to achieve zero-downtime deployments. Combine with feature flags to control rollout.
example: Use Kubernetes rolling update with readinessProbe and feature flag toggles for gradual release.

title: Normalization (1NF/2NF/3NF)
content: Normalization is the process of organizing tables to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. Common forms are 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependencies), and 3NF (no transitive dependencies).
example: Split Customer and Orders into two tables: Customers(Id, Name, ...) and Orders(Id, CustomerId, OrderDate, ...) with CustomerId FK to Customers.

title: Indexes (Clustered vs Non-Clustered)
content: Clustered index defines physical row order (one per table). Non-clustered indexes are separate structures that speed reads for specific columns. Use indexes to improve SELECTs but avoid excessive indexing for writes.
example: CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Id ON Orders(Id); CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerId ON Orders(CustomerId);

title: Execution Plans and Query Tuning
content: Execution plans show how SQL Server executes a query. Use Actual Execution Plan to spot scans, expensive operators, missing indexes, and high-cost joins. Tune queries by rewriting, indexing, or updating statistics.
example: SET STATISTICS IO ON; SET STATISTICS TIME ON; -- run query and view plan in SSMS or Azure Data Studio

title: Transactions and Isolation Levels
content: Transactions ensure atomicity across multiple statements. Isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, SERIALIZABLE) balance consistency vs concurrency and control phenomena like dirty reads and phantom reads.
example: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE Id = 1; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 100 WHERE Id = 2; COMMIT;

title: Deadlocks and detection/handling
content: Deadlocks occur when two sessions hold locks the other needs. SQL Server detects deadlocks and kills a victim. Prevent by keeping transactions short, accessing objects in consistent order, and using appropriate lock hints when necessary.
example: Use extended events or trace flag 1222 to capture deadlock graph; redesign transactions to access tables in same order to avoid deadlocks.

title: Stored Procedures vs Functions
content: Stored procedures can perform actions and return result sets; they may have side effects. Functions (scalar/table-valued) are meant to be side-effect free and can be used in queries. Choose based on need for side-effects, performance, and composability.
example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrders @CustId INT AS SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = @CustId; CREATE FUNCTION dbo.TotalOrders(@CustId INT) RETURNS INT AS BEGIN RETURN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId=@CustId); END;

title: ACID Properties
content: ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) are guarantees provided by the database transaction system to ensure reliable processing of transactions.
example: Use BEGIN TRAN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK to ensure a multi-step payment operation is atomic and durable.

title: Temp Tables vs Table Variables
content: Temp tables (#temp) are created in tempdb, support statistics and indexing, and are better for larger datasets. Table variables (@table) have more limited optimization but lower overhead for small data. Choose based on volume and need for statistics.
example: CREATE TABLE #Tmp (Id INT); INSERT INTO #Tmp SELECT Id FROM Orders; -- vs DECLARE @Tmp TABLE (Id INT);

title: Backup and Restore Strategies
content: Implement full, differential, and transaction-log backups to meet RPO/RTO. Test restores regularly and use restore with STOPAT for point-in-time recovery when using full recovery model.
example: BACKUP DATABASE MyDb TO DISK='C:\backups\MyDb_full.bak'; BACKUP LOG MyDb TO DISK='C:\backups\MyDb_log.trn'; RESTORE DATABASE MyDb FROM DISK='...';

title: Always On Availability Groups / High Availability
content: Availability Groups provide high availability and read-scale by replicating databases to secondary replicas. Configure failover modes, readable secondaries, and proper backups on secondary where supported.
example: CREATE AVAILABILITY GROUP [AG1] ... -- configure replicas and listener in SQL Server and Windows/cluster or Azure SQL Managed Instance

title: Parameter Sniffing
content: Parameter sniffing is when SQL Server caches a plan optimized for the first execution parameters which may be suboptimal for others. Mitigate using plan hints, OPTIMIZE FOR, RECOMPILE, or plan guides.
example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = @CustId OPTION (RECOMPILE); -- avoids reuse of a bad cached plan

title: Statistics and Maintenance
content: Statistics inform the optimizer about data distribution. Keep statistics up to date and reorganize/rebuild indexes regularly to maintain performance. Use AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS and schedule maintenance windows for index rebuilds.
example: UPDATE STATISTICS Orders; ALTER INDEX ALL ON Orders REBUILD;

title: Partitioning Tables
content: Table partitioning splits large tables into smaller segments by key (e.g., date) improving manageability and performance for large datasets (partition elimination, faster archiving).
example: CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION pfDateRange (DATE) AS RANGE LEFT FOR VALUES ('2020-01-01','2021-01-01'); CREATE PARTITION SCHEME psDateScheme AS PARTITION pfDateRange ALL TO ([PRIMARY]);

title: Query Hints and When to Use Them
content: Query hints (e.g., FORCESEEK, NOLOCK, MAXDOP) override optimizer behavior. Use sparingly and only after understanding costs; hints can improve a specific query but may degrade others.
example: SELECT * FROM Orders WITH (FORCESEEK) WHERE OrderDate > '2024-01-01';
